title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
This page (pp. 96-97 of Novi Commentarii X, 1766, E297) is the historical and conceptual introduction to Euler's analytic exposition of Lagrange's δ-method.

End of §III. For an ordinary function V(x,y), the problem 'maximize V at x=a' is solved by fixing x=a and finding a single number y. For the integral A=∫_0^a Z dx this does not work. The value A depends on the whole relation y=y(x), through all the 'intermediate values' of y, so the unknown is a relation (a function), not a number.

§IV. Z may be any function of x, y, p=dy/dx, q=dp/dx, r=dq/dx, …, i.e. derivatives of arbitrary order. It may even contain embedded integral formulas, i.e. nonlocal functionals. This yields several classes of problems to which the method must be adapted.

§V. History as Euler gives it:
- Such problems began with Jakob Bernoulli's isoperimetric problem.
- Bernoulli's method covered only Z(x,y,p) and had to be rederived geometrically for each special case.
- Euler then found a fully general method, covering derivatives of every order and integral formulas, and set it out in a separate book (the Methodus inveniendi, 1744).

§VI. Euler's methodological criticism:
- His own method needs no figures when applied, but was derived from contemplating curves, so it did not seem 'natural' to him.
- Since the problem can be posed without geometry, an adequate solution from true principles should be free of geometry.
- He had voiced this wish in the treatise. Lagrange ("de la Grange Tournier") wrote to him from Turin that he had fulfilled it, and sent the foundations of his analysis.
- Euler resolves (on the next page) to explain and develop it in his own manner.

No computations appear on this page.
errors: No mathematical errors. Euler's account is historically compressed: Johann Bernoulli's work, Euler's own earlier papers (E27, E56) and Lagrange's 1755 letter and 1762 Miscellanea Taurinensia paper are not dated or detailed. Bernoulli's methods were not strictly limited to first-order Lagrangians in all respects, but the characterization is the standard one.

ideas.what: A maximization problem for an integral has a function (a relation between x and y) as its unknown, not a value; the integral depends on all intermediate values of y.
ideas.modern_name: Functional on a function space; calculus of variations vs. ordinary extremum problems

ideas.what: Integrands depending on derivatives of arbitrary order and on embedded integral formulas
Methodological demand that the solution be purely analytic, free of geometric considerations, crediting Lagrange's Turin letter for fulfilling it
ideas.modern_name: Origin of the δ-calculus / 'calculus of variations' as a purely analytic discipline
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (letter of 12 Aug 1755; Misc. Taur. 1762); Euler's naming in E296/E297
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum, E297; Euler-Lagrange correspondence (Opera omnia IVa.5)

deep.surprise_reason: A well-known historical preface: Euler credits Lagrange and explains the shift from his geometric method to the analytic δ-method. It is thoroughly discussed by Goldstine, Fraser and Carathéodory's Opera omnia introduction. Nothing new.
transcription_corrections: The transcription of p.97 begins 'tate a Viro illo' while the image shows 'sagacitate' split across pages as 'sagaci-/tate'; this is fine.
'de la Grange Tournier' is faithful to the print ('Tournier' for Lagrange's Turin-derived name); no correction needed.
